prior.t: Before reading an email, **40 of every 100** are spam. So our starting belief, the **prior, is P(spam) = 0.4**. It is a belief held **before** looking at this email's words.

evidence.t: Now the email arrives and it contains the word **“free”**. That is the evidence. **30 of the 100** emails contain it (outlined).

likelihood.h: THE LIKELIHOOD: EVIDENCE GIVEN THE CAUSE
likelihood.t: We can measure how often spam contains “free”: **24 of the 40 spam emails**, so **P(free | spam) = 0.6**. This is the likelihood. Only 6 of 60 normal emails contain it: **0.1**.

reverse-condition.t: We know **P(free | spam)**: from the cause to the evidence. But what we want is **P(spam | free)**: from the evidence back to the cause. **Bayes' rule turns one arrow around.**

normalize.t: How often does “free” show up at all? From spam: **0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24**. From normal mail: **0.1 × 0.6 = 0.06**. Together **P(free) = 0.30**. Dividing by it makes the two explanations share the evidence fairly.

posterior.t: **P(spam | free) = likelihood × prior / evidence = 0.6 × 0.4 / 0.30 = 0.24 / 0.30 = 0.8.** This is the **posterior**, the belief after seeing the evidence.

compare-before-after.t: The belief moved from **0.4 (prior) to 0.8 (posterior)**. The evidence was stronger for spam than for normal mail, so it pushed the belief up.

ml-connection.t: A **naive Bayes classifier** does exactly this: it estimates priors and likelihoods from data, then computes the posterior for each new email and **predicts the more probable class**.
